replies:
Good — you’re at final rounds with Lincoln International for an analyst role. I’ll prep you for the likely interview structure, give high-impact questions and model answers, list what to emphasize about your profile, and a 10-point quick plan for the next 48 hours. I assumed this is an on-site or virtual final-round with 2–4 interviewers including a senior banker; tell me if it’s actually a case/slide presentation or a technical modeling test and I’ll tailor it.
1) What to expect (likely)
- 2–4 interviews: behavioral + fit, technical finance/modeling, deal discussion / market knowledge, and culture/team fit with a senior person.
- They’ll test: transaction experience (deal role, process), modeling and valuation basics (LBO, DCF, comps), commercial judgment (industry questions), and how you handle pressure / client interactions.
- Time: 30–60 minutes per interviewer. Bring crisp stories and be ready to build or walk through numbers on a whiteboard or screen share.
2) Top things to demonstrate (short)
- Transaction clarity: your exact role, tasks you owned, decisions you influenced, outcome and metrics.
- Modeling competence: you can explain mechanics and assumptions clearly (drivers, sensitivities, terminal value), and you can spot obvious mistakes.
- Commercial sense: industry drivers, buyer motivations, value creation levers.
- Team fit and stamina: attention to detail, responsiveness, client-facing readiness.
- Curiosity and humility: ask smart questions, acknowledge limits, offer how you’d find answers.
3) Five behavioral stories to prepare (structure: Situation, Task, Action, Result with numbers)
Prepare 2–3 minute STAR answers for each:
- Lead/ownership under pressure: e.g., took lead on a deadline-critical model fix; what you did, edits made, result (closed on time, saved fee).
- Dealing with ambiguity: built a valuation or market case with limited data; how you sourced assumptions, triangulated comps, outcome.
- Team conflict / feedback: a time you disagreed with senior analyst and how you resolved it; keep it professional.
- Failure + learning: a mistake in work or model, how you corrected it, and what process you changed.
- Client interaction or presentation: input you prepared for senior review or client slide deck and the impact.
4) Top technical topics and how to answer crisply
- DCF: Explain steps (forecast cash flows, discount rate/WACC, terminal value via exit multiple or Gordon growth), what drives value (growth, margins, capex, WACC), and sensitivity testing.
- LBO basics: sources & uses, purchase price, financing stack, debt paydown, IRR drivers (entry/exit multiple, leverage, margin expansion), covenants to watch.
- Comparable company / precedent transactions: when to use each, pros/cons, choice of multiple (EV/EBITDA, EV/Revenue).
- Working capital mechanics: why negative/positive WC matters, how it flows to cash.
- Quick mental math: be ready to sanity-check multiples, implied enterprise value, or IRR roughs on the spot.

Model answer snippets you can practice (2–3 sentences each)
- “Walk me through a DCF.” — “We project unlevered free cash flow for 5–7 years from revenue growth less operating costs, capex and changes in working capital; discount at WACC to get NPV and add terminal value (exit multiple or perpetuity). Key sensitivities: revenue growth, margin expansion and discount rate — small changes in these drive most valuation moves.”
- “How does an LBO generate IRR?” — “IRR comes from paying down debt and exiting at a higher multiple or with greater EBITDA — so return drivers are leverage at entry, EBITDA growth, margin improvement and multiple expansion at exit. Cash flow must cover interest and mandatory amortization.”
- “Tell me about a deal you worked on.” — Use STAR: “We advised [buyer/seller], I owned the 3-statement model and comps, identified a working-capital risk that reduced base-case proceeds by 8%, advised adjusting the SPA language; the deal closed at X% above the initial bid.”
5) Deal discussion checklist (what to have ready for their deal questions)
- One or two deals you worked on, with: your exact title and responsibilities, deal rationale, valuation range, your model inputs and one surprise or complication you handled.
- An example of a valuation sensitivity you ran and why it changed the recommendation.
- One question you would ask a client in that industry today (shows curiosity).
6) Questions they will ask you (practice these aloud)
- Why Lincoln International? — Short: specific firm strengths (mid-market focus, global cross-border capabilities, culture). Tie to your experience and what you can add.
- Why investment banking / analyst role? — Brief motivation (transaction work you’ve done, quantitative rigor, client advisory interest).
- Tell me about a time you did [X: modeling, team leadership, client work]. — Use STAR with numbers.
- Walk me through your resume — 2–3 minute narrative linking prior roles to this role.
- Where do you see yourself in 2–3 years? — Focus on learning, technical mastery, contributing to deals.
7) Questions to ask them (good to end with)
- Ask about typical deal team structure and what success looks like for an analyst in first 12 months.
- Ask about the firm’s recent mid-market trends or a notable recent transaction and what the team learned.
- Ask about mentorship, training, and feedback cadence.
8) Quick 10-point prep plan (next 48 hours)
1. Pick and rehearse 3 deal stories using STAR with exact numbers and your role. (I can turn one into a 2-minute script.)
2. Refresh one LBO and one DCF in 15–20 minutes each; prepare to sketch them on screen/whiteboard.
3. Run through the model sanity checks: EBITDA → EV via multiples, quick IRR back-of-envelope.
4. Practice 6 behavioral Qs aloud; time answers to 90–150 seconds.
5. Prepare a 2–3 minute resume walkthrough linking jobs chronologically.
6. Draft 2–3 firm-specific lines: why Lincoln (tie to mid-market/global work or recent deal).
7. Prepare 3 smart questions for interviewers (team, deals, coaching).
8. Sleep, and have logistics set: charger, quiet room, printouts if on-site.
9. Prepare one failure + learning story — be concise and concrete.
10. If there’s a live modeling test: ensure your software works and you can share screen; if in-person, bring printed model copies.

9) Short mock question to start practice now
Practice this answer aloud: “Tell me about a time you improved a model or process under a tight deadline.” Reply with your 60–90 second answer and I’ll score it and give one concrete fix, then provide the next question.

One question: is your final round virtual or in-person, and will there be a modeling or presentation component? That changes what I make you rehearse first.

You don't have any postings or applications on file yet. The one step that starts this is: paste the job link or tell me the company and exact job title for the "first one" you mean.

When you give one posting, I'll prepare an application card for your approval. Here exactly is what I'll fill and submit onto the card, field by field, using only the posting's text and your confirmed facts (I'll mark anything missing in [brackets] so you can supply it):
- Employer (company): exact company name as the posting shows.
- Role / job title: exact job title from the posting.
- Location and work arrangement: city/state or "Remote"/"Hybrid"/"On-site" exactly as the posting states.
- Job link: the employer's link for this posting (what you pasted).
- Pay: the posting's stated pay (or "not listed" if it doesn't state pay).
- Resume to send: the resume persona or file name you'll choose (default: your active resume). If you haven't set a resume contact I'll ask: "What name and email should go at the top of your resume?" That exact name/email will be used.
- Cover note / short message (under 120 words): a 1–3 sentence tailored opener that I will draft using the posting's keywords and your confirmed facts. Any missing personal points will be shown in [brackets].
- Screening question answers: precise answers to each required screening question the posting asks (I will draft them; any dates, salary history, or facts not on file will be in [brackets]).
- Work authorization / visa status: one-line statement (I will put [Your work authorization] if you haven't confirmed it).
- Earliest start date: I'll use [earliest start date] unless you tell me now.
- Portfolio / attachments: list of additional files the posting requests (portfolio link, code sample, certifications). I'll list what I will attach and show the attachments for you to confirm.
- References: I'll note "References available on request" unless you type names/emails now; I never add names without your explicit text.
- Phone and contact email: taken from the resume contact you set; if none set, I'll ask for the exact name and email to use.
- Equal Opportunity / EEO statements: copied from the posting into the card where required.
- Notes / flags for you: any hard requirements you don't meet (e.g., required years, certifications), and the exact language I used to tailor the cover note and screening answers (keywords and achievements called out).
- Attachments checklist: the exact list of files that'll be attached (resume file name, portfolio link, certificates). I will not attach anything you haven't confirmed.
- Final preview text: the full short cover note and every screening answer, shown for your review before anything is queued.
What I will not do without your approval:
- I will not queue or submit the application automatically. After preparing the card, I will show you the complete card with any [bracketed] missing items. You must approve each card in the extension before it is queued or sent.

Next step: paste the job link or type the company and exact title for the "first one" and I will read it and prepare the card as described. Saved: nothing yet. Is that the right next step?
